questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Getting an opportunity to understand central/Eastern European way of life

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: That was not a hassle. but a tip would be to write down all dates in your calendar the second you know them.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The necessary. All things uni-related was in English, but don't expect people outside uni to be able to help in English.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy - you just sign up a couple months before

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The metro is great - live near a stop if you're not close to the centre.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The dorms are generally not good. I arrived late, and there were no double rooms left, so I got a single room, which is the only reason I didn't move out of the Hvezda dorms.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You have to sign up at very specific times. The Czech students have priority for the courses, so there's a good chance you don't get a spot where you want. Then you can sign up for a waiting list (everyone were on waiting lists), and you might get a spot. 
You have two weeks or so, to try out the courses (you can attend more than you plan on following) and then you have to decide which to follow. This is a very useful way of choosing, since the course descriptions rarely reflect the teaching methods, level, expectations etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always write or call the coordinator

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got what I thought I wanted - turned out the courses were not as well-taught as I expected in some cases.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Register for a lot of courses that you might think are interesting, and attend the first lecture(s) before deciding what to follow.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level can be divided into two categories; teaching and expectations. The quality of the teaching was rarely up to the standard that KU students will be used to, but luckily the level of expectations is generally not either.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Not a lot of exercises or group work. There is a lot more hierarchy between students and lecturers. In two of my courses, they tried to cover a completely unreasonable amount of topics, leading to very superficial knowledge of each topic, and they rarely made it through all of the prepared material, before the lecture was over.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Economics of green deal (ba), Behavioral Economics (ba), Energy security in Israel and the Middle East (ma), Financial accounting (ba), European economic integration (ba), Understanding a small state: The Czech Republic in a nutshell (ba)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Energy security in Israel and the Middle East (ma): Very well taught, very engaging teacher, Interesting for both political science and economy, 4 ects in an intense week of teaching
Behavioral Economics (ba): Every week was a new topic, and the teaching was based on a couple interesting first hand studies every time.
Understanding a small state: The Czech Republic in a nutshell (ba): Nice course if you want to learn basic czech history, economy, politics etc.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Weekly runs and other sports activities
Usually something going on at campus hybernska

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join the buddy programme

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There's a huge difference between Prague and the rest of the republic, both culturally, but also socio-economically. Explore the rest of the country to see this, and go see the beautiful nature

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Semi - in the start I often got tired of the nonexistence of English in the (large) bureaucracy that entangles many things

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join the buddy program

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: the (large) bureaucracy

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People seemed less stressed

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Join the buddy program
If you plan on living at the dorms with a random roommate, know that you might want to move after a while
You are probably a year or two older than most other exchange students from other countries. At times, they seem a lot younger, so you might want to try and make some friends that are also your age.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The campuses are not very close to each other at all - be aware of this when trying to make your schedule.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends we made along the way...

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Trying to figure out how much was expected of us for the exam.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
